column9: Match each term about oxygen and fermentation to its meaning.
column14: Aerobic :: Uses oxygen
column15: Anaerobic :: Does not use oxygen
column16: Fermentation :: The anaerobic process that follows glycolysis
column17: Pyruvate :: The molecule glycolysis makes from glucose
column28: Aerobic means with oxygen and anaerobic means without oxygen ('an-' = without). When there is no oxygen, pyruvate from glycolysis goes into fermentation instead of the mitochondria.
column29: 'Aero' has to do with air. The prefix 'an-' means 'without'.

column9: When your muscle cells run low on oxygen and switch to fermentation, what do they produce?
column14: Lactic acid
column15: Ethanol
column16: Citric acid
column17: Glucose
column28: Human muscle cells do lactic acid fermentation: pyruvate → lactic acid. Ethanol is made by yeast, citric acid is part of the Krebs cycle, and glucose is the fuel, not the product.
column29: It is the acid that makes your legs burn during a hard workout.

column9: In alcoholic fermentation, yeast turn pyruvate into an alcohol called ___.
column28: Yeast turn pyruvate into ethanol (ethyl alcohol, C₂H₅OH) and carbon dioxide. That is why it is called alcoholic fermentation.
column29: Look back at the alcoholic fermentation equation in your notes. The alcohol is the product that is NOT a gas.

column9: Using Mr. Erickson's numbers, how many ATP does anaerobic respiration make from one glucose?
column28: Anaerobic respiration makes only 2 ATP per glucose (from glycolysis). Aerobic respiration makes 36.
column29: Fermentation only keeps the ATP that glycolysis makes.

column9: Where in the cell does anaerobic respiration happen?
column14: Mitochondria
column15: Nucleus
column16: Cytoplasm
column17: Chloroplast
column28: Anaerobic respiration happens entirely in the cytoplasm: glycolysis, then fermentation. Pyruvate never enters the mitochondria, which are only used when oxygen is present.
column29: Without oxygen, pyruvate stays where glycolysis happened.

column9: True or false: Lactic acid fermentation produces carbon dioxide.
column28: False. Lactic acid fermentation makes lactic acid and 2 ATP, with no CO₂: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + 2 ATP. Alcoholic fermentation (yeast) is the kind that makes CO₂.
column29: Compare the two fermentation equations. Which one has CO₂ on the right side?

column9: Bread dough rises because of bubbles made by yeast. What gas fills those bubbles?
column14: Oxygen
column15: Carbon dioxide
column16: Nitrogen
column17: Hydrogen
column28: Yeast doing alcoholic fermentation give off carbon dioxide (CO₂). The gas gets trapped in the dough and makes it rise. Oxygen is not made by fermentation.
column29: Alcoholic fermentation makes ethanol and one gas. Which gas?

column9: Which process produces carbon dioxide, water, and ATP?
column14: Lactic acid fermentation
column15: Alcoholic fermentation
column16: Photosynthesis
column17: Aerobic respiration
column28: Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + ATP. Neither kind of fermentation makes water, and photosynthesis uses up carbon dioxide and water instead of making them.
column29: Recall each equation. Which one has 6H₂O on the products side?

column9: True or false: Both aerobic and anaerobic respiration begin with glycolysis.
column28: True. Glycolysis (glucose → pyruvate in the cytoplasm) is the first step of both. What happens to the pyruvate next depends on whether oxygen is present.
column29: Does glycolysis need oxygen?

column9: Which activity depends **most** on anaerobic respiration?
column14: Sleeping through the night
column15: An all-out 100 m sprint
column16: Walking slowly to class
column17: Reading a book in study hall
column28: A short, all-out sprint needs ATP faster than your blood can deliver oxygen, so muscles switch to lactic acid fermentation. Sleeping, walking, and reading use little energy, so aerobic respiration keeps up easily.
column29: Which activity would leave your legs burning and out of breath?

column9: Which organisms use aerobic respiration?
column14: Animals, but not plants, which make their own food
column15: Animals that have lungs, but not fish or insects
column16: Mainly microbes such as yeast and bacteria
column17: Plants, animals, and many fungi and bacteria
column28: Plants, animals, and many fungi and bacteria use aerobic respiration when oxygen is available. Plants make their own food by photosynthesis but still break it down in their mitochondria. Cells, not lungs, do respiration, so fish and insects use it too. Yeast and bacteria use it, but they are far from the only ones.
column29: Do plant cells have mitochondria too?

column9: What is the main advantage of aerobic respiration over anaerobic respiration?
column14: It makes much more ATP from each glucose
column15: It does not need any glucose to run
column16: It works without any oxygen at all
column17: It makes lactic acid to power muscles
column28: Aerobic respiration makes about 36 ATP per glucose, compared with only 2 for anaerobic respiration. Both use glucose, aerobic needs oxygen, and lactic acid is a waste product of anaerobic respiration.
column29: Which process keeps going in the mitochondria after glycolysis?

column9: True or false: Your muscle cells can switch to anaerobic respiration when they are not getting enough oxygen.
column28: True. During hard exercise, if oxygen can't reach muscle cells fast enough, they switch to lactic acid fermentation so they can keep making a little ATP.
column29: What happens in your legs at the end of a hard sprint?

column9: In Mr. Erickson's notes, how many ATP does **aerobic** respiration make from one glucose?
column28: Aerobic respiration makes 36 ATP per glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + 36 ATP.
column29: It is the number written at the end of the aerobic respiration equation.

column9: Which of these is an **anaerobic** process?
column14: Krebs cycle
column15: Electron transport chain
column16: Lactic acid fermentation
column17: Pyruvate moving into the mitochondria
column28: Lactic acid fermentation happens without oxygen, so it is anaerobic. The Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, and pyruvate moving into the mitochondria are all steps of aerobic respiration that only happen when oxygen is present.
column29: Which of these can happen when no oxygen is present at all?

column9: Which equation shows **lactic acid fermentation**?
column14: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + ATP
column15: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP
column16: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + ATP
column17: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
column28: Lactic acid fermentation: glucose → 2 lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃) + ATP. It uses no O₂ and makes no CO₂, and choices a, b, and d all have CO₂ in them.
column29: Lactic acid fermentation has no oxygen going in and no CO₂ coming out.

column9: Which equation shows **alcoholic fermentation** in yeast?
column14: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + ATP
column15: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + ATP
column16: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP
column17: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 2C₂H₅OH + ATP
column28: Alcoholic fermentation: glucose → 2 ethanol (C₂H₅OH) + 2 CO₂ + ATP. Fermentation uses no O₂, so c and d are out, and b makes no ethanol and no CO₂.
column29: Fermentation never takes in oxygen. Which product makes alcoholic fermentation different from lactic acid fermentation?

column9: Which statements are true of **both** aerobic and anaerobic respiration? Select all that apply.
column14: They break down glucose
column15: They make ATP
column16: They require oxygen
column17: They take place entirely in the mitochondria
column18: They produce the same amount of ATP per glucose
column28: Both break down glucose, both make ATP, and both happen in living cells. Only aerobic respiration needs oxygen, uses the mitochondria, and makes 36 ATP; anaerobic stays in the cytoplasm and makes only 2.
column29: For each statement, ask: is this also true when there is NO oxygen?

column9: Match each situation to the process that is happening.
column14: Arms burning at the end of a long wrestling match :: Lactic acid fermentation
column15: Bread dough rising on the counter :: Alcoholic fermentation
column16: Jogging slowly for 30 minutes :: Aerobic respiration
column28: Burning muscles come from lactic acid building up during hard work. Rising dough comes from CO₂ made by yeast in alcoholic fermentation. A slow, steady jog gets enough oxygen for aerobic respiration.
column29: Which one involves yeast? Which one gets plenty of oxygen?

column9: Why do muscle cells switch to anaerobic respiration during intense exercise?
column14: Lungs stop taking in oxygen during very hard exercise
column15: Muscle cells save their oxygen for after the race
column16: Lactic acid blocks oxygen from entering muscle cells
column17: Muscles use oxygen faster than the blood can deliver it
column28: During intense exercise, muscles use oxygen faster than the blood can supply it, so they switch to lactic acid fermentation to keep making some ATP. Your lungs keep taking in oxygen (you breathe harder), cells don't save oxygen for later, and lactic acid causes fatigue but doesn't block oxygen from getting into cells.
column29: Think about supply and demand for oxygen during a sprint.

column9: Why does aerobic respiration make so much more ATP than anaerobic respiration?
column14: Aerobic respiration starts with much more glucose
column15: Pyruvate continues on to the Krebs cycle and ETC
column16: Anaerobic respiration happens in the mitochondria
column17: Lactic acid is used to make extra ATP right away
column28: With oxygen, pyruvate goes into the mitochondria, where the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain pull out much more energy (36 ATP total). Without oxygen, the process stops after glycolysis and fermentation (2 ATP). Both start with one glucose.
column29: Which stages only happen when oxygen is present? Which stage makes the most ATP?

column9: Using Mr. Erickson's ATP numbers, how many **times as much** ATP does aerobic respiration make per glucose as anaerobic respiration?
column28: Aerobic respiration makes 36 ATP per glucose and anaerobic makes 2. 36 ÷ 2 = 18, so aerobic makes 18 times as much ATP from each glucose.
column29: Recall the ATP per glucose for each process. 'How many times as much' means divide the bigger number by the smaller one.

column9: Yeast cells in a sealed jar ferment **50** glucose molecules with no oxygen. How many ATP do they make in all?
column28: Fermentation makes 2 ATP per glucose. 50 × 2 = 100 ATP.
column29: How many ATP does one glucose make without oxygen? Multiply.

column9: In the Muscle Fatigue Lab, Carter squeezed a clothespin 42 times in trial 1, 31 times in trial 5, and 22 times in trial 10, with no rest. What is the best explanation?
column14: His muscles made more ATP with each new trial
column15: His muscles ran out of carbon dioxide to use
column16: His muscles stopped doing glycolysis after trial 1
column17: His muscles ran low on oxygen and lactic acid built up
column28: With no rest, his finger muscles used oxygen faster than it could be delivered, so they switched to lactic acid fermentation. Lactic acid built up and the muscles fatigued, so his squeezes dropped. ATP went down, not up; muscles don't use CO₂; and glycolysis keeps going.
column29: Think about what the muscles were short of, and what that leads to.

column9: After the Muscle Fatigue Lab, Sophie's fingers work normally again after about 10 minutes of rest. Why?
column14: Her fingers made new glucose from carbon dioxide
column15: Oxygen returns, and the lactic acid is broken down
column16: Lactic acid turned into ethanol and evaporated
column17: Her muscles switched from aerobic to anaerobic
column28: While she rests, blood brings oxygen back to the muscles. Aerobic respiration starts again and the lactic acid is broken down, so the fatigue goes away. Muscles can't make glucose from CO₂, human cells don't make ethanol, and resting switches muscles back TO aerobic.
column29: What does the muscle get back when it rests, and what happens to the waste?

column9: Grace puts yeast, sugar, and warm water in a flask and seals it with a balloon. No air can get in. The balloon slowly inflates. What is happening?
column14: Yeast are doing photosynthesis and giving off O₂
column15: Yeast are breaking down water into hydrogen gas
column16: Yeast are fermenting the sugar and giving off CO₂
column17: The warm water is boiling and making steam
column28: Once the little oxygen trapped in the flask is used up, the yeast do alcoholic fermentation: sugar → ethanol + CO₂ + 2 ATP. The CO₂ gas fills the balloon. Yeast are fungi and cannot do photosynthesis, yeast don't split water into hydrogen gas, and warm (not boiling) water doesn't make enough steam to inflate a balloon.
column29: Yeast + sugar + no oxygen = which process? Which product is a gas?

column9: Which statement correctly compares **where** aerobic and anaerobic respiration happen?
column14: Aerobic: cytoplasm, then mitochondria. Anaerobic: cytoplasm only
column15: Aerobic: mitochondria only. Anaerobic: cytoplasm only
column16: Aerobic: cytoplasm only. Anaerobic: mitochondria only
column17: Both: cytoplasm first, then into the mitochondria
column28: Both start with glycolysis in the cytoplasm, so aerobic respiration is not mitochondria-only. With oxygen, pyruvate then moves into the mitochondria for the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain. Without oxygen, pyruvate stays in the cytoplasm for fermentation and never enters the mitochondria.
column29: Glycolysis happens in the same place for both. Where does the pyruvate go next?

column9: To make yogurt, bacteria are added to warm milk. A few hours later the milk is thick and tastes sour. What made it sour?
column14: Bacteria fermented the milk sugar into lactic acid
column15: Bacteria made ethanol and CO₂ by fermentation
column16: Bacteria made CO₂ and water by aerobic respiration
column17: Bacteria used up the oxygen, which made the milk sour
column28: Yogurt bacteria break down milk sugar by lactic acid fermentation, and the lactic acid makes the milk sour and thick. Ethanol and CO₂ come from alcoholic fermentation, which is done by yeast, not yogurt bacteria. Aerobic respiration makes CO₂ and water, not a sour acid. Running out of oxygen has no taste of its own; the sourness comes from the acid the bacteria make.
column29: Which type of fermentation happens in some bacteria and in your muscles?

column9: True or false: A marathon runner jogging at a steady pace gets most of her ATP from aerobic respiration.
column28: True. At a steady pace, her blood delivers enough oxygen for aerobic respiration, which makes 36 ATP per glucose. That is how she can keep going for hours. Fermentation takes over mostly during short, all-out bursts.
column29: Can she get enough oxygen at a steady jog? Which process could last for hours?

column9: Put the events in order for a runner doing an all-out sprint.
column14: Her muscle cells switch to fermentation
column15: She rests and breathes hard, and the waste is broken down
column16: The runner starts sprinting as hard as she can
column17: A waste product builds up and her legs burn
column18: Her muscle cells use oxygen faster than the blood can deliver it
column28: The sprint starts, oxygen demand passes the supply, the cells switch to fermentation, lactic acid builds up and burns, and then rest and heavy breathing bring oxygen back so the lactic acid is broken down.
column29: Think cause and effect: each event is caused by the one before it.

column9: Which statement correctly compares how bread and yogurt are made?
column14: Bread: bacteria doing lactic acid fermentation. Yogurt: yeast doing alcoholic fermentation
column15: Bread: yeast doing lactic acid fermentation. Yogurt: bacteria doing alcoholic fermentation
column16: Bread: yeast doing alcoholic fermentation. Yogurt: bacteria doing lactic acid fermentation
column17: Bread: yeast doing alcoholic fermentation. Yogurt: yeast doing alcoholic fermentation
column28: Bread rises because yeast do alcoholic fermentation, and the CO₂ bubbles get trapped in the dough. Yogurt is made by bacteria doing lactic acid fermentation, and the lactic acid makes the milk thick and sour. Choice a flips both the microbes and the processes, choice b gives each microbe the wrong process, and choice d forgets that yogurt is made by bacteria, which make lactic acid, not ethanol.
column29: Which microbe makes the gas bubbles in bread dough? Which kind of fermentation makes milk turn sour?

column9: Your red blood cells have no mitochondria. So they make all of their ATP by ___ respiration, even though they carry oxygen around your body.
column28: Anaerobic. Aerobic respiration needs mitochondria for the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain. With no mitochondria, red blood cells can only do glycolysis and fermentation in the cytoplasm. That is anaerobic respiration (lactic acid fermentation, the same kind your muscles use when they run short of oxygen), so they get just 2 ATP per glucose. They deliver oxygen to other cells but don't use it to make their own ATP.
column29: Which stages of respiration happen inside the mitochondria? Without them, how far can a cell break glucose down?

column9: Kayla is filling in the **Reactants** row of a table comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration. Which entry is correct?
column14: Aerobic: glucose only. Anaerobic: glucose and oxygen
column15: Aerobic: glucose and oxygen. Anaerobic: glucose only
column16: Aerobic: glucose and oxygen. Anaerobic: glucose and CO₂
column17: Aerobic: CO₂ and water. Anaerobic: glucose only
column28: Aerobic respiration takes in glucose and oxygen (C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → …). Anaerobic respiration takes in glucose alone, with no oxygen. CO₂ and water are products of aerobic respiration, not reactants, and fermentation never takes in oxygen or CO₂.
column29: Reactants go on the left side of an equation. Which process's name tells you it needs something besides glucose?

column9: Some bacteria are **anaerobic**. Where would they most likely live and grow?
column14: Near the air bubbler in a fish tank
column15: In a fast, splashing mountain stream
column16: On a leaf in a sunny garden
column17: Deep in the mud at the bottom of a pond
column28: Anaerobic means without oxygen, so anaerobic bacteria make their ATP without it and live where oxygen is missing, such as deep mud. A fish-tank bubbler and a splashing stream both mix air into the water, and a leaf in the sun gives off oxygen from photosynthesis, so all three places have plenty of oxygen.
column29: What does the prefix 'an-' mean? Which place would have the least oxygen?

column9: True or false: Fermentation lets cells keep making a small amount of ATP when oxygen runs out.
column28: True. Fermentation lets glycolysis keep running without oxygen, so the cell still makes 2 ATP per glucose. It is a backup plan, not a replacement for aerobic respiration.
column29: Without fermentation, would the cell make any ATP at all when oxygen is gone?

column9: Which product is made by aerobic respiration **and** alcoholic fermentation, but **not** by lactic acid fermentation?
column14: Lactic acid
column15: Carbon dioxide
column16: Water
column17: Ethanol
column28: Aerobic respiration makes CO₂, water, and ATP. Alcoholic fermentation makes ethanol, CO₂, and ATP. Lactic acid fermentation makes only lactic acid and ATP. CO₂ is the only product made by the first two but not by lactic acid fermentation. ATP is made by all three, water is only aerobic, ethanol is only alcoholic, and lactic acid comes only from lactic acid fermentation.
column29: Write out all three sets of products and look for the one in the first two lists only.

column9: After months of cross-country training, Emma's leg muscles fatigue much more slowly. Which change in her muscle cells best explains this?
column14: They have fewer mitochondria and more lactic acid
column15: They now make ethanol instead of lactic acid
column16: They have stopped doing glycolysis at all
column17: They have more mitochondria for aerobic respiration
column28: Regular exercise makes muscle cells build more mitochondria. More mitochondria means more aerobic respiration (36 ATP per glucose) and less need for fermentation, so lactic acid builds up more slowly. Human cells can't make ethanol, and glycolysis is always the first step.
column29: Which organelle lets a cell make lots of ATP with oxygen?

column9: Yeast in rising bread dough also make an alcohol. Why does baked bread contain almost none of it?
column14: Most of the alcohol evaporates in the oven's heat
column15: The alcohol turns into the gas that makes dough rise
column16: Kneading the dough squeezes the alcohol out
column17: The yeast turn the alcohol back into sugar
column28: Yeast do make alcohol (ethanol) as the dough rises, but ethanol boils at a lower temperature than water, so the oven's heat drives most of it off. The gas and the alcohol are separate products of fermentation, kneading can't squeeze out a liquid mixed through the dough, and yeast don't turn alcohol back into sugar.
column29: Think about what an oven's heat does to a liquid like alcohol.

column9: Avery's Muscle Fatigue Lab data. Dominant hand squeezes: 45, 41, 36, 30, 26 | Non-dominant hand squeezes: 38, 33, 27, 22, 18 (trials 1 to 5). Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Only the non-dominant hand got tired over the five trials
column15: The dominant hand got stronger as the trials went on
column16: Both hands tired over time; the dominant hand did more each trial
column17: Both hands stayed about the same from trial to trial
column28: Both lists go down every trial (fatigue from lactic acid buildup), and the dominant hand's number is higher in every trial. Neither hand got stronger or stayed the same.
column29: Check whether each list goes up or down, then compare the two lists trial by trial.

column9: In trial 1 of the Muscle Fatigue Lab, Liam squeezed 40 times. In trial 10 he squeezed 28 times. By what **percent** did his squeezes decrease?
column28: Change = 40 − 28 = 12. Percent decrease = 12 ÷ 40 × 100 = 30%.
column29: Find the change first, then divide by the starting value and multiply by 100.

column9: A cell has **10** glucose molecules. How many **more** ATP will it make if it uses aerobic respiration instead of anaerobic respiration? Use Mr. Erickson's ATP numbers.
column28: Aerobic: 10 × 36 = 360 ATP. Anaerobic: 10 × 2 = 20 ATP. Difference: 360 − 20 = 340 more ATP.
column29: Find the total ATP each way first, then subtract.

column9: Flask A has yeast, sugar, and warm water. Flask B has yeast and warm water but **no sugar**. Each is sealed with a balloon. Only balloon A inflates. What can you conclude?
column14: Yeast make CO₂ from warm water alone
column15: Sugar kills yeast and stops respiration
column16: Yeast need sugar as fuel to make CO₂
column17: The balloons are the cause of the CO₂
column28: The only difference between the flasks is sugar, and only the flask with sugar made gas. So the yeast needed sugar (glucose) as the fuel for fermentation, which gives off CO₂. Flask B shows water alone doesn't work, and sugar clearly didn't stop the yeast in flask A.
column29: What is the one difference between the flasks? Which flask made gas?

column9: A sprinter's muscle cells and the yeast in bread dough both ferment glucose, but they end up with different products. Where do the two processes become different?
column14: In what the pyruvate from glycolysis is turned into
column15: In how much oxygen each type of cell uses
column16: In how much ATP they make: 36 for yeast, 2 for muscle
column17: In glycolysis, which muscle cells skip but yeast do not
column28: Both start the same way: glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate and makes 2 ATP. The difference comes next, in what the pyruvate is turned into: muscle cells make lactic acid, while yeast make ethanol and CO₂. Fermentation uses no oxygen, both make only 2 ATP, and neither skips glycolysis.
column29: Both start the same way. Follow the glucose step by step and find the first step that is different.

column9: Tyler says, "Anaerobic respiration doesn't need oxygen, so my muscles should just use it all the time." Which response is best?
column14: He's right; anaerobic respiration makes more ATP than aerobic
column15: He's right; lactic acid gives muscles extra energy to use
column16: It can't work in humans because only yeast do fermentation
column17: It makes far less ATP, and lactic acid causes fatigue
column28: Anaerobic respiration is a short-term backup. It makes only 2 ATP per glucose (vs. 36), and lactic acid builds up and causes muscle fatigue. Humans can do lactic acid fermentation, but not for long.
column29: Compare the ATP each makes, and think about how your legs feel after fermenting.

column9: Isaac tests yeast in sealed bottles at different temperatures. Data table: Temperature (°C): 5, 25, 40, 60 | Balloon width (cm): 1, 8, 15, 0. Which explanation fits the data best?
column14: Colder temperatures always make yeast work faster
column15: Warmth speeds fermentation, but 60 °C killed the yeast
column16: Temperature had no effect on the amount of CO₂
column17: Yeast made the most CO₂ at the hottest temperature
column28: Balloon size grows from 5 °C to 40 °C, so warmth sped up fermentation. At 60 °C there was no gas at all, so the heat killed the yeast (their enzymes stopped working). This is why yeast set-ups use warm water, not hot water: 60 °C is far below boiling, but it was still hot enough to kill the yeast.
column29: Follow the numbers from left to right. What happens at the very last temperature?

column9: Yeast can do aerobic respiration or fermentation. Bottle 1 of yeast and sugar water is open to the air. Bottle 2 is sealed, and its yeast soon use up the oxygen inside. Which statement correctly compares the two bottles?
column14: Only Bottle 1 must ferment, because open air makes yeast switch to fermentation
column15: Only Bottle 2 must ferment, so its yeast get more ATP from each glucose
column16: Neither must ferment; Bottle 2's yeast just stop making ATP until air returns
column17: Only Bottle 2 must ferment, so its yeast get less ATP from each glucose
column28: Bottle 2 has no oxygen left, so its yeast can't do aerobic respiration and must switch to alcoholic fermentation, which makes only 2 ATP per glucose instead of 36. Bottle 1's yeast have oxygen, so they are not forced to ferment. Open air doesn't cause fermentation, and yeast without oxygen don't simply stop: fermentation keeps a little ATP coming.
column29: Which process needs a reactant that one bottle no longer has? Then compare the ATP the two processes make.

column9: Oxygen is removed from each organism's surroundings. Which one would **not** be able to survive?
column14: Yeast in a jar of warm sugar water
column15: A mouse in a cage with food and water
column16: Bacteria living deep in pond mud
column17: Yogurt bacteria in a cup of warm milk
column28: A mouse needs a lot of ATP for its brain, heart, and body heat, and fermentation's 2 ATP per glucose can't keep it alive for more than a few minutes. Yeast can switch to alcoholic fermentation, mud bacteria live without oxygen, and yogurt bacteria get their ATP from lactic acid fermentation.
column29: For each organism, ask: does it have a way to make enough ATP with no oxygen?

column9: Ryan wants to test whether the amount of sugar affects how much CO₂ yeast make. Tube 1 gets 1 g sugar in warm water. Tube 2 gets 3 g sugar in cold water. What is wrong with his experiment?
column14: He should have used the same amount of sugar
column15: He should have measured oxygen, not CO₂
column16: He changed two variables, sugar and temperature
column17: Nothing; this is a fair test of sugar amount
column28: A fair test changes only one variable (the independent variable: sugar). Ryan also changed the temperature, so if the tubes differ he can't tell which change caused it. Temperature should be a constant. Using the same sugar would remove his independent variable.
column29: How many things are different between Tube 1 and Tube 2?

column9: Coach says Ty's leg muscles switched to anaerobic respiration in the last 200 m of his 800 m race. Which observations support this? Select all that apply.
column14: His legs started to burn
column15: His leg muscles got weaker and slower
column16: He kept breathing hard for minutes after he finished
column17: His leg muscles started to give off ethanol
column18: His legs felt fresher and stronger than at the start
column28: Burning legs, weaker and slower muscles, and hard breathing that lasts after the race (his body repaying the oxygen his muscles were short) all point to lactic acid fermentation. Human muscle cells make lactic acid, not ethanol, and fermentation causes fatigue, not fresher, stronger legs.
column29: Think about how your legs feel when lactic acid builds up and what your body needs afterward. Which product do human cells make?

column9: A muscle needs 432 ATP for a workout. How many **more** glucose molecules would it have to break down using anaerobic respiration than using aerobic respiration?
column28: Anaerobic: 432 ÷ 2 = 216 glucose. Aerobic: 432 ÷ 36 = 12 glucose. Difference: 216 − 12 = 204 more glucose. Fermentation needs 18 times as much glucose to make the same ATP (18 is how many times as much, not how many more).
column29: Find how many glucose each process needs to make 432 ATP, then subtract.
